Reward shaping interference in multi-task RLHF asks whether, when a single value function approximator is trained jointly across tasks with distinct human preference signals, the gradient updates from one task's reward model systematically distort the value landscape of another — not through catastrophic forgetting, but through a subtler corruption of the shaped reward surface itself. The core tension is that reward shaping (adding potential-based or learned auxiliary terms to guide policy optimization) is theoretically conservative under single-task assumptions — Ng et al.'s potential-based shaping preserves optimal policy invariance — but this guarantee dissolves when the shaping terms are themselves learned functions sharing parameters with a multi-task critic. A beginner sees multi-task RLHF as a straightforward extension: more tasks, more signal, better generalization. An expert worries that policy gradient cross-contamination occurs when the advantage estimates for task A are computed using a value baseline that has been shifted by reward model gradients from task B, producing biased gradient directions that are neither task-A-optimal nor task-B-optimal but a nonsensical composite — particularly dangerous when tasks have conflicting preference geometries (e.g., a helpfulness reward that rewards verbosity conflicting with a conciseness reward). The shared value function essentially acts as an unintended communication channel between tasks, smuggling reward signal across task boundaries in ways that are invisible to standard per-task evaluation metrics, meaning interference can be severe and persistent without any per-task performance collapse serving as a diagnostic signal.

The task-conditioning mechanism dominates over width or depth as the primary determinant of interference dynamics, because it controls the degree to which task identity information is entangled with value estimates in the shared representation. Additive task embeddings — where a learned task vector is simply summed with the state encoding before the critic head — are the most pathological configuration: the gradient of the value loss with respect to shared trunk parameters receives contributions from all tasks simultaneously, with no architectural barrier preventing task B's preference geometry from rotating the shared feature directions that task A's policy gradient depends on. By contrast, FiLM-style conditioning (feature-wise linear modulation, as used in several multi-task RL systems including work from the DeepMind control suite generalization benchmarks) applies per-task affine transforms at each layer, which empirically reduces but does not eliminate cross-task gradient alignment, because the trunk weights themselves still accumulate mixed-task curvature in the Hessian. Hypernetwork conditioning — where a task-specific network generates the critic's weights entirely — is the structural extreme that most approaches self-cancellation, at the cost of parameter explosion and reduced transfer of genuinely shared value structure. Width matters secondarily: a wider trunk increases the probability that orthogonal subspaces exist for different tasks' gradient directions (a consequence of the blessing of dimensionality in high-dimensional parameter spaces, formalized in the context of multi-task learning by Yu et al.'s PCGrad, 2020), but width cannot compensate for additive conditioning because the entanglement occurs before the nonlinearity stack has any chance to decorrelate representations. Depth interacts with conditioning placement: conditioning injected only at the input layer propagates interference through every subsequent layer's Jacobian, whereas mid-network conditioning (as in some variants of multi-task PPO critics) contains contamination to the upper trunk, leaving lower-layer features more task-agnostic and stable.

The mechanism is curvature domination: the Hessian of the shared trunk loss is a sum of per-task Hessian contributions, and because the Hessian's spectral norm scales roughly with the square of the gradient magnitude, tasks with higher reward variance produce larger gradient second moments, causing their curvature to dominate the eigenspectrum of the joint Hessian and effectively warping the loss landscape for all other tasks. Concretely, if task A's reward model outputs are high-variance (say, a helpfulness scorer with output std ~3.0) and task B's are low-variance (a safety classifier with output std ~0.4), the Fisher information matrix — which approximates the Hessian under natural gradient methods and is used explicitly in TRPO and implicitly shaped by Adam's second moment estimates — will be ~56x more heavily weighted toward task A's curvature directions, meaning the effective learning rate for task B's value signal is suppressed in precisely those parameter directions where task A has high curvature. FiLM's affine transforms modulate activations post-hoc but don't alter the trunk weight gradients themselves, so the trunk's Adam optimizer accumulates a second-moment estimate that reflects the mixture of task gradient variances rather than any per-task decomposition — this is the residual interference FiLM cannot eliminate. The asymmetry compounds across training steps because Adam's β₂ (typically 0.999) means the second-moment buffer has an effective memory of ~1000 steps, so early high-variance task gradients continue to suppress low-variance task updates long after the reward distributions might have shifted. (2019) on Multinet and Yu et al.'s PCGrad both document that gradient magnitude imbalance, not gradient direction conflict alone, is the primary driver of asymmetric task interference, with the lower-variance task reliably underfitting relative to its single-task baseline. The practical consequence for RLHF is that safety-relevant reward signals — which human annotators tend to apply more consistently and with lower variance than helpfulness signals — are systematically underfit in joint training, a failure mode invisible to aggregate reward metrics but detectable in per-task advantage estimate calibration.

Gradient surgery at the optimizer level — PCGrad's projection of conflicting task gradients onto each other's normal planes, or the more aggressive CAGrad's constrained optimization formulation — does not resolve asymmetric Hessian accumulation because it operates on the first-moment (gradient direction) interference while leaving the second-moment buffer entirely untouched; Adam still accumulates a blended curvature estimate across all tasks regardless of whether the gradients were projected before the parameter update. The new interference surface introduced at the projection step is subtle but consequential: PCGrad's conflict detection uses cosine similarity between task gradient vectors, which is a scale-invariant measure, meaning it will project away directional conflicts between a high-variance task A gradient and a low-variance task B gradient even when the correct resolution is not projection but re-weighting — the projection can actually amplify the effective update magnitude imbalance by removing the component of the low-variance gradient that happened to align with the high-variance gradient's direction, leaving a residual that is both smaller and potentially pointing in a less useful direction for task B. Farajtabar et al.'s Orthogonal Gradient Descent (2020) and the subsequent IMTL-G (Liu et al., 2021) attempted to address this by normalizing gradient magnitudes before conflict resolution, achieving more symmetric effective learning rates across tasks, but both methods assume that the optimal resolution of gradient conflict is a convex combination lying on the Pareto front of task losses — an assumption that breaks down precisely in RLHF settings where the reward models themselves are non-stationary and the "true" Pareto front shifts during training. A deeper problem is that gradient surgery is applied per-step to instantaneous gradient estimates, but the Hessian interference is a cumulative phenomenon living in the optimizer state — there is a temporal mismatch between the intervention timescale and the accumulation timescale, so even perfect per-step gradient surgery cannot undo the curvature bias already encoded in Adam's β₂ buffer from prior steps. The most honest empirical verdict comes from Kurin et al. (2022), who showed in controlled multi-task RL experiments that gradient surgery methods produce inconsistent gains and sometimes hurt performance relative to simple loss re-weighting, precisely because they solve the wrong interference surface while leaving optimizer-state contamination intact; the implication for multi-task RLHF is that per-task Adam buffers — maintained separately per task with shared gradient signals only at the parameter update step — are likely a more targeted fix than any gradient projection scheme.

Per-task Adam buffers stabilize value learning for the tasks whose reward models are stationary but introduce a specific destabilization pathology for the task undergoing reward model update: the curvature estimate in that task's buffer was accumulated under the old reward model's loss landscape, and when the reward model shifts, the buffered second moments reflect a curvature geometry that is now stale — Adam will apply inappropriately large or small effective learning rates in parameter directions whose importance has changed, a problem structurally identical to the "optimizer state invalidation" issue documented in continual learning literature under the term plasticity loss. The severity scales with how abruptly the reward model changes: iterative RLHF pipelines that update reward models in discrete rounds (as in Anthropic's early RLHF work and the InstructGPT pipeline) create step-function non-stationarity where the mismatch between buffered curvature and true curvature is maximized immediately post-update, whereas continuously updated reward models (online RLHF variants) produce slower curvature drift that the buffer can partially track if β₂ is tuned aggressively downward. The interaction with multi-task dynamics is that the stale-buffer task will temporarily exhibit inflated or deflated advantage estimates — because the value function is being updated with miscalibrated effective learning rates — and these miscalibrated values bleed into the policy gradient even for other tasks if the policy shares parameters, creating a transient cross-task interference spike that per-task buffers were supposed to eliminate but actually concentrate and then discharge unevenly. A concrete mitigation is partial buffer reset on reward model update events: zeroing the second-moment buffer for the affected task forces Adam to behave like SGD with a warm-up phase, accepting higher variance updates initially in exchange for rapid curvature re-estimation under the new reward landscape — this is analogous to the "warm restart" strategy in learning rate scheduling (SGDR, Loshchilov & Hutter 2017) but applied selectively to optimizer state rather than learning rate. The deeper instability, however, is that partial resets break the theoretical convergence guarantees Adam relies on (monotonically non-decreasing second-moment estimates), and in practice the reset task's value loss can spike transiently by 2-5x before re-stabilizing, during which policy gradient updates for that task are effectively driven by a poorly conditioned critic — suggesting that reward model update scheduling, not just optimizer design, must be treated as a first-class variable in multi-task RLHF system design.

The least-studied failure mode is preference gradient collision at the reward model embedding layer: when two reward models share a pretrained language model backbone (as is common in parameter-efficient RLHF setups using LoRA or shared frozen encoders with task-specific heads), simultaneous updates on conflicting annotation batches produce opposing gradient signals on the shared token representations, and the resulting parameter update is not a principled compromise but an arithmetic average of incompatible preference directions that satisfies neither task's annotation signal — this is distinct from the value function interference discussed earlier because it corrupts the reward signal itself before it ever reaches the critic. The interference manifests primarily in the reward models rather than the value function or policy, but through a non-obvious pathway: the conflicting gradients don't cancel cleanly because annotation batches are rarely balanced in sequence length, token distribution, or preference margin, meaning the gradient magnitudes are asymmetric and the "average" update systematically biases toward whichever task had higher-margin preference pairs in that batch — a phenomenon with no standard diagnostic because per-task reward model accuracy metrics will both appear stable while the shared embedding has drifted toward one task's preference geometry. This embedding drift then propagates downstream with a one-round delay: the corrupted reward model produces shifted scalar rewards in the next RLHF iteration, which enter the replay buffer and corrupt value function training before any per-task monitoring would flag anomalous reward distributions, creating a latency between cause and observable effect that makes attribution nearly impossible post-hoc. The policy is the last to show symptoms and the most misleading diagnostic: it will adapt to the drifted reward signal and appear to improve on aggregate metrics while actually having learned a mixed preference representation that neither human annotator group would endorse, analogous to the mode-averaging failures documented in reward model ensembling literature (Coste et al., 2023 on reward model ensembles for overoptimization). Staggered reward model updates — updating task A's reward model, running one full value function synchronization step, then updating task B's — would eliminate simultaneous gradient collision at the embedding layer, but this scheduling constraint has not been systematically studied in any published multi-task RLHF framework, and the optimal stagger interval almost certainly depends on the KL divergence between tasks' annotation distributions in a way that requires per-deployment empirical calibration rather than a universal recipe.

Annotator calibration variance functions exactly as a hidden hyperparameter controlling backbone drift, and the mechanism is precise: reward models trained with cross-entropy on Bradley-Terry preference pairs produce gradient magnitudes proportional to the preference margin (the difference in log-probabilities assigned to chosen vs. rejected responses), so a task whose annotators consistently assign high-confidence labels (e.g., 90/10 splits) produces gradients roughly 4x larger than a task whose annotators hedge (60/40 splits), even when both tasks have identical dataset sizes and ostensibly equal weight in the joint training objective. This is not a theoretical concern — Ziegler et al. (2019) and subsequent InstructGPT ablations both note that reward model training is sensitive to label noise and annotator disagreement, but neither work studied the multi-task case where the calibration asymmetry between tasks is the operative variable rather than noise within a single task; the multi-task case is strictly worse because the asymmetry is structured and persistent rather than random and self-averaging. The drift dynamic under systematic annotator confidence asymmetry becomes self-reinforcing: the high-confidence task's gradients dominate the shared embedding, which causes the backbone to represent that task's semantic distinctions more faithfully, which in turn makes the reward model more accurate for that task's future annotation batches, potentially increasing apparent annotator agreement and thus margin — a feedback loop that concentrates representational capacity in the dominant task while the low-confidence task's reward model quietly degrades. Critically, this failure is invisible to standard inter-annotator agreement metrics computed per-task: task B's annotators may genuinely disagree at 60/40 rates due to task ambiguity rather than poor calibration, so the low confidence is epistemically appropriate, yet the shared backbone still treats it as a weaker training signal and under-allocates representational resources accordingly. The implication is that annotator calibration variance must be explicitly estimated and compensated — either through per-task gradient re-weighting inversely proportional to mean preference margin (a form of task-aware loss scaling not currently standard in any published RLHF pipeline), or through annotator-level temperature calibration as studied by Bakker et al. (2022) in the context of value pluralism in RLHF, extended to the multi-task setting where the calibration correction must be applied before gradients reach the shared backbone rather than post-hoc on reward outputs.

Yes, the destructive interaction is real and follows directly from how the KL penalty enters the PPO objective: the KL term β·KL(π||π_ref) is typically applied with a single global β coefficient, so when inverse-margin re-weighting amplifies the low-confidence task's reward gradients to match the high-confidence task's influence, the policy update magnitude for the low-confidence task increases without any corresponding increase in its KL budget — the same β that was calibrated for the original gradient scale now under-penalizes KL divergence relative to the amplified reward signal, meaning the low-confidence task's policy should actually drift more freely post-re-weighting, not less. The over-regularization failure you describe runs in the opposite direction and emerges from a subtler interaction: if the re-weighting is applied at the reward model training level but the PPO rollouts still use the original (pre-re-weighted) reward scalar to compute advantages, the advantage estimates for the low-confidence task remain small in absolute magnitude, and since the KL penalty is subtracted from the reward in absolute terms (r - β·KL), the penalty consumes a disproportionate fraction of the low-confidence task's effective reward signal, pushing the policy toward the reference model not because of over-regularization in principle but because the reward-to-KL ratio is structurally unfavorable. This reward-to-KL ratio imbalance is precisely what Stiennon et al. (2020) observed informally in summarization RLHF when reward scale varied across domains, and it motivated the use of reward normalization before PPO training — but in the multi-task case, normalizing rewards per-task before PPO would undo the gradient re-weighting intended to compensate for annotator calibration asymmetry, creating a circular dependency between the re-weighting intervention and the normalization intervention. The high-confidence task drifts freely under this configuration because its reward-to-KL ratio remains favorable even under global β: its large absolute reward signals dominate the KL penalty term, and its policy explores aggressively, potentially entering reward-hacking regimes that the low-confidence task's over-constrained policy never reaches — producing a within-training divergence in policy behavior across tasks that aggregate KL metrics will not detect because they average across tasks. The principled resolution requires per-task β coefficients scaled proportionally to each task's effective reward variance after re-weighting, as suggested implicitly by the adaptive KL controller in the original InstructGPT (which adjusted β dynamically based on observed KL divergence) — but extending this to per-task adaptive controllers in a shared-policy multi-task setting introduces a new scheduling problem: the controllers will fight over the shared policy's KL budget, and without a global constraint on the sum of per-task KL penalties, the system has no mechanism to prevent the total policy drift from exceeding safe bounds.
